segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is a mile from the Bell to Oakmere gate, east along the Alresford road, and Nathaniel Farr had walked it in the dark at nineteen with a soldier's bounty in his pocket and his great-uncle shouting after him from the yard. The hedges were cut lower now. Somebody had grubbed out the crab tree at the bend, which he minded more than he expected to.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The gate was new and hung true. Beyond it the house sat where it had always sat, red brick going brown, with the pear trained flat along the south wall and smoke standing straight up out of the kitchen chimney into a still October afternoon. There were curtains in the two front windows. They were yellow, and looped back with cord, and behind them was the room in which Aldous Fenner had sat for forty years with the shutters half closed because he could not abide a draught.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A dog he did not know came off the step and barked at him. The door opened before he reached it.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: Down. Down, sir. He is quite harmless. You will be Captain Farr.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: Well. This is a surprise. I do not say it is not a very great surprise. We had you dead these three years, you know, and half the county with us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was fair, and soft in the hand, and dressed for a street in town rather than a farmyard in Hampshire, with a watch-chain hung where a man could not fail to see it. He stood in the middle of the doorway. He did not move out of it.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: I wrote twice from Lisbon. The letters went astray with the regiment. I am sorry for the trouble of it.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: Not at all, not at all. You must let me condole with you. He went off very easy at the end, they tell me, and knew nobody by the last week. You will have heard about the will.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: In the coach yard. Not an hour ago.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: Then you had better see it, and we shall have no awkwardness between us. Wait there a moment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went in and left the door ajar, and came back with a folded paper which he opened against the door frame, holding it so that Farr might read it and not take hold of it. It was dated the fourteenth of September. Everything of which Aldous Fenner died possessed, the land, the stock, the hop ground, the whole three hundred a year of it, went to Vernon Hartwell. Underneath were two signatures in the hands of servants.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: Witnessed by his own people, you observe. Dorcas Whitlow, that has kept his house thirty years, and Thomas Ames from the dairy. No stranger came near him.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: He told me the farm was mine. Standing in that yard, the night before I went for a soldier. He said it before witnesses of his own choosing and he said it in the shop in the village and he said it, I do not doubt, to half the parish.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: I am sure he did. An old man says a great many kind things, Captain, and I would not have you think me hard for saying so. Have you it in writing?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a pause of some length.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Mr Vernon Hartwell
segments.text: There it is, then. You will not think me uncivil if I do not ask you in. The house is at sixes and sevens, painters in the back passage, and Mrs Whitlow scarcely knows where anything is put. Come another day and we shall drink his memory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The door shut. Not hard; that was the worst of it. Farr stood in his great-uncle's yard until the dog lost interest in him, and then he turned and went back down the track toward the road, and it was in turning that he looked up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the upper window over the porch a woman was watching him. Grey hair under a plain cap, and a hand pressed flat to the glass. Thirty years she had known him, and she had fed him bread and dripping in that kitchen when he was a boy, and her name was on the paper he had just been shown. She did not open the casement. She did not lift the hand. She stood quite still and let him go.
